title: Tesla’s Flying Car and the Trouble With Success

body.text: Tesla’s new “flying car” would be terrible at flying you to work. That might also be the least interesting thing about it.

On October 15, Tesla showed an unmanned Roadster prototype clinging upside down to a curved structure using suction fans, then jumping and rotating with compressed-gas thrusters. It was spectacular, but not sustained flight, and certainly not proof of what a production model will deliver.
Musk was explicit about one part of the appeal: the car “takes the fun meter to 11 out of 10.” That’s a different pitch from an airborne commute.
A shared deliverable isn’t the same as a shared definition of success.

That’s a familiar BA problem. One stakeholder imagines a breakthrough experience, another expects practical functionality, a third wants a viable business outcome. If those expectations stay implicit, everyone can approve the same requirement and picture a different finish line. Defining success means agreeing beforehand on the outcome, the constraints, and the evidence that would prove it. Fun is a legitimate product goal. It doesn’t settle safety, practicality, or commercial viability. A remarkable demo answers “can it do this?”
Success starts with “what did we actually want?”
